subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about the results of the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford alpha-particle scattering experiment is correct?
items.correct: Nearly all the alpha particles passed through almost undeflected; a very few were deflected by more than 90°.
items.misconception: Most of the alpha particles were deflected through large angles, and only a few passed straight through.
items.why:
Textbook diagrams and animations of the experiment draw attention to the few alpha particles that bounce back, often showing several rebounding paths, and Rutherford's much-quoted remark about a shell bouncing off tissue paper makes the rebound the memorable result. Count the outcomes: nearly every alpha particle went through almost undeflected. The surprise was that ANY bounced back, not that many did. Both facts matter: the rare large deflections show the positive charge is concentrated; their rarity shows the nucleus is tiny.

Working: No calculation is needed. The results: almost all alpha particles passed through the foil with little or no deflection; a very small fraction were deflected through large angles, some through more than 90°.
items.specStatementText: the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment and the discovery of the nucleus
items.random_wrong: The few alpha particles that bounced back had collided with the electrons in the gold atoms.
items.working: No calculation is needed. The results: almost all alpha particles passed through the foil with little or no deflection; a very small fraction were deflected through large angles, some through more than 90°.

items.q: What did Rutherford conclude about the structure of the atom from the results of the Geiger–Marsden experiment?
items.correct: Its positive charge and nearly all its mass are in a tiny central nucleus.
items.misconception: Its nucleus consists of protons and neutrons, which the experiment first detected.
items.why: Textbooks present the nuclear atom as a finished picture, protons and neutrons in a nucleus with electrons outside, immediately after describing the experiment, so the whole picture is credited to it. Separate what the evidence shows from what was learned later. The scattering pattern depends only on the nucleus's total charge and on it being small and massive; it says nothing about what particles the nucleus contains.
items.specStatementText: the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment and the discovery of the nucleus
items.random_wrong: It is a solid ball, and most alpha particles passed through the gaps between the atoms.

items.q: A nucleus of potassium-40 is written in nuclear notation as ⁴⁰₁₉K. Which statement about this nucleus is correct?
items.correct: It contains 21 neutrons.
items.misconception: It contains 40 neutrons.
items.why:
The proton number already counts protons, so students assume the other number counts the other particle; the older term 'mass number' also hides that A includes the protons. A nucleon is either a proton or a neutron, and A counts both. Subtract the proton number: N = A − Z.

Working: A = 40 (upper number), Z = 19 (lower number). Protons = 19; nucleons = 40; neutrons N = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.
items.specStatementText: nuclear notation ᴬ_Z X where A is the nucleon number Z is the proton number and X is the chemical symbol
items.random_wrong: It contains 19 neutrons.
items.working: A = 40 (upper number), Z = 19 (lower number). Protons = 19; nucleons = 40; neutrons N = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.

items.q: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are two isotopes of chlorine. A chlorine-35 nucleus contains 17 protons. Which statement about a chlorine-37 nucleus is correct?
items.correct: It contains 17 protons and 20 neutrons.
items.misconception: It contains 19 protons and 18 neutrons.
items.why:
Students learn that isotopes 'have different mass numbers' without linking the proton number to the identity of the element, so any change in the nucleus seems possible. The proton number defines the element. Change it and you have a different element; isotopes keep Z and differ only in N.

Working: Isotopes of one element have the same proton number, so Z = 17 for both. Chlorine-35: N = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons. Chlorine-37: N = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons, two more than chlorine-35.
items.specStatementText: nuclear notation ᴬ_Z X where A is the nucleon number Z is the proton number and X is the chemical symbol
items.random_wrong: It contains 17 protons and 18 neutrons.
items.working: Isotopes of one element have the same proton number, so Z = 17 for both. Chlorine-35: N = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons. Chlorine-37: N = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons, two more than chlorine-35.

items.q: The emission spectrum of a hot, low-pressure gas of one element consists of bright lines at a set of separate wavelengths. Why is this evidence that the atoms have discrete energy levels?
items.correct: Each line has a single photon energy, equal to the difference between two of the atom's allowed energies.
items.misconception: Each line has the photon energy of one allowed level, so each line marks one energy level.
items.why: Energy-level diagrams show each level with its own energy value and spectra show separate lines, so students pair one line with one level instead of with a pair of levels. A line is produced by a transition between two levels, and ΔE = E_upper − E_lower = hf. An atom with several levels can make more lines than it has levels, because every pair of levels can give a line.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide evidence for discrete atomic energy levels
items.random_wrong: The lines are equally spaced in frequency, just as the atom's energy levels are equally spaced.

items.q: White light, containing all visible wavelengths, passes through a cool gas of a single element and is then examined with a spectrometer. What is observed?
items.correct: Dark lines at wavelengths that match some of the element's emission lines.
items.misconception: Dark lines at wavelengths that differ from all of the element's emission lines.
items.why: Absorption and emission spectra look like opposites (dark lines on a bright background, bright lines on a dark background), and students carry the idea of 'opposite' over to the wavelengths. A photon absorbed in a transition between two levels has exactly the energy of the photon emitted in the reverse transition, ΔE = hf, so the same wavelengths appear in both spectra.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide evidence for discrete atomic energy levels
items.random_wrong: A dark band across every wavelength shorter than the one for the smallest energy gap.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how an atom emits a photon?
items.correct: An electron moves to a lower energy level and one photon carries away the energy lost.
items.misconception: An electron moves to a higher energy level and one photon carries away the energy gained.
items.why: An 'excited' atom sounds energetic and active, so emission is linked with the excitation itself; 'jump' also suggests the electron's energy is released as it moves. Apply conservation of energy: a higher level has more energy, so getting there needs an input; dropping to a lower level releases the energy difference as a photon.
items.specStatementText: that photons are emitted and absorbed during atomic transitions
items.random_wrong: An electron leaves the atom altogether, and that electron is itself the photon that is detected.

items.q: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV (the ground state), −5.0 eV and −3.0 eV. An atom in its ground state is struck by a photon of energy 3.0 eV. What happens?
items.correct: The photon is not absorbed, as it matches neither gap from the ground state, 5.0 or 7.0 eV.
items.misconception: The photon is not absorbed, as it matches neither gap from the ground state, 15.0 or 13.0 eV.
items.why:
Subtracting a negative number is error-prone, and students who drop the minus signs of both levels, or write −3.03 − 5.14, end up adding the magnitudes. Keep the signs: ΔE = E_final − E_initial. The level nearer zero is the higher level; the difference is always smaller than the magnitude of the lower level.

Working: Photon energies that can be absorbed from the ground state: exactly −5.0 − (−10.0) = 5.0 eV or −3.0 − (−10.0) = 7.0 eV for excitation, or at least 0 − (−10.0) = 10.0 eV for ionization. 3.0 eV is neither, so the photon is not absorbed. (The atom is in the ground state, so the 2.0 eV gap between −5.0 eV and −3.0 eV is not available either, and it does not equal 3.0 eV.)
items.specStatementText: that photons are emitted and absorbed during atomic transitions
items.random_wrong: The photon is absorbed, and the electron moves up to the −3.0 eV energy level.
items.working: Photon energies that can be absorbed from the ground state: exactly −5.0 − (−10.0) = 5.0 eV or −3.0 − (−10.0) = 7.0 eV for excitation, or at least 0 − (−10.0) = 10.0 eV for ionization. 3.0 eV is neither, so the photon is not absorbed. (The atom is in the ground state, so the 2.0 eV gap between −5.0 eV and −3.0 eV is not available either, and it does not equal 3.0 eV.)

items.q: In a sodium atom, an electron makes a transition from an energy level at −3.03 eV to one at −5.14 eV. What is the frequency of the emitted photon? Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
items.why:
Energy levels are quoted in eV throughout, and students treat the eV as just another energy unit without checking consistency with the units of h. Check units: f = E/h has units J/(J s) = s⁻¹ only if E is in joules. 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Working: ΔE = E_upper − E_lower = (−3.03) − (−5.14) = 2.11 eV. In joules: 2.11 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.376 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE/h = 3.376 × 10⁻¹⁹ J / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s = 5.09 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
items.specStatementText: that the frequency of the photon released during an atomic transition depends on the difference in energy level as given by E = hf

items.q: An atom has only three energy levels: −1.00 eV, −3.00 eV and −7.00 eV. What is the energy of the emitted photon that has the SHORTEST wavelength?
items.why:
Students picture a longer wave as 'bigger' and therefore more energetic, as with a longer spring or a bigger ocean wave. Use E = hc/λ: energy and wavelength are inversely proportional. Blue light (short λ) has more energy per photon than red light (long λ).

Working: Downward transitions and photon energies: −1.00 → −3.00 eV: 2.00 eV; −3.00 → −7.00 eV: 4.00 eV; −1.00 → −7.00 eV: 6.00 eV. Since λ = hc/E, the largest photon energy, 6.00 eV, gives the shortest wavelength.
items.specStatementText: that the frequency of the photon released during an atomic transition depends on the difference in energy level as given by E = hf
items.working: Downward transitions and photon energies: −1.00 → −3.00 eV: 2.00 eV; −3.00 → −7.00 eV: 4.00 eV; −1.00 → −7.00 eV: 6.00 eV. Since λ = hc/E, the largest photon energy, 6.00 eV, gives the shortest wavelength.

items.q: The spectrum of light from a star shows strong dark lines at exactly the wavelengths of the two bright yellow lines in the laboratory emission spectrum of sodium. What can be concluded from this evidence?
items.correct: Sodium atoms in the star's outer layers absorb light at these wavelengths, so sodium is present in the star.
items.misconception: Sodium is absent from the star, because the light at sodium's wavelengths is missing from its spectrum.
items.why: A missing colour is read as a missing ingredient, and bright lines are associated with 'the element being there' from flame tests and emission spectra. Match dark lines to laboratory emission lines. A dark line means atoms that absorb that wavelength lie between the source and the observer, so the element is present.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide information on the chemical composition.
items.random_wrong: Nothing about sodium, because an element absorbs at different wavelengths from those it emits.

items.q: A nucleus of lead-208 has proton number 82 and nucleon number 208. Using R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, what is the radius of this nucleus?
items.why:
Students expect 'twice as many particles' to make everything twice as big, without distinguishing length from volume. Nucleons are packed like marbles in a bag: doubling the number doubles the volume, and volume ∝ R³, so R ∝ A^(1/3).

Working: R = R₀A^(1/3) = (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)(208)^(1/3) = (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)(5.925) = 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the radius and the nucleon number for a nucleus as given by R = R₀A^(1/3) and implications for nuclear densities

items.q: Nuclear radii are given by R = R₀A^(1/3), and the mass of a nucleus may be taken as proportional to its nucleon number A. What is the ratio (density of a carbon-12 nucleus)/(density of a molybdenum-96 nucleus)?
items.why:
Students conflate 'heavy' with 'dense', as when a lead ball is described as heavier than an aluminium one of the same size. Density is mass per unit volume. Adding nucleons adds mass and volume in the same proportion, so the density does not change.

Working: Density ρ = m/V with m ∝ A and V = ⁴⁄₃πR³ = ⁴⁄₃πR₀³A, so ρ ∝ A/A, the same for every nucleus. ρ(carbon-12)/ρ(molybdenum-96) = (12/12)/(96/96) = 1.00. (Numerically, ρ = 3 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/(4π × (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)³) = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ for both.)
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the radius and the nucleon number for a nucleus as given by R = R₀A^(1/3) and implications for nuclear densities
items.working: Density ρ = m/V with m ∝ A and V = ⁴⁄₃πR³ = ⁴⁄₃πR₀³A, so ρ ∝ A/A, the same for every nucleus. ρ(carbon-12)/ρ(molybdenum-96) = (12/12)/(96/96) = 1.00. (Numerically, ρ = 3 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/(4π × (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m)³) = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ for both.)

items.q: In alpha-particle scattering, the numbers scattered through large angles agree with Rutherford's prediction, which assumes that only the electric repulsion acts, at low energies. At kinetic energies of a few tens of MeV the measured numbers fall below the prediction. What is the reason?
items.correct: The alpha particles get close enough to the nucleus to feel the short-range strong nuclear force.
items.misconception: Gravitational attraction between the alpha particles and the very massive nucleus becomes significant.
items.why: The nucleus is described as containing nearly all the atom's mass, and students often assume that gravity is what holds nucleons together. Compare the forces: gravity depends on masses of about 10⁻²⁵ kg and is tiny. The forces that matter inside a nucleus are the electric force and the strong nuclear force.
items.specStatementText: deviations from Rutherford scattering at high energies
items.random_wrong: The strong nuclear force, reaching far beyond the nucleus, now outweighs the electric force.

items.q: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV moves head-on towards a gold-197 nucleus (proton number 79). Only the electric repulsion acts, and the recoil of the nucleus is negligible. The radius of a nucleus is R₀A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach?
items.why:
Students think of the alpha particle as 'a positive particle' and use the familiar value e, as for a proton. Count the protons: an alpha particle is a helium nucleus with Z = 2, so q = 2e.

Working: E_k = 5.0 MeV = 5.0 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J. At closest approach E_k = kqQ/d with q = 2e, Q = 79e. d = kqQ/E_k = (8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)(3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1.264 × 10⁻¹⁷ C)/(8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J) = 3.636 × 10⁻²⁶ J m/8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J = 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. (Nuclear radius R₀A^(1/3) = 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so the alpha particle never reaches the nucleus.)
items.specStatementText: the distance of closest approach in head-on scattering experiments
items.working: E_k = 5.0 MeV = 5.0 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J. At closest approach E_k = kqQ/d with q = 2e, Q = 79e. d = kqQ/E_k = (8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)(3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1.264 × 10⁻¹⁷ C)/(8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J) = 3.636 × 10⁻²⁶ J m/8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J = 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. (Nuclear radius R₀A^(1/3) = 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so the alpha particle never reaches the nucleus.)

items.q: Alpha particles of kinetic energy E_k are fired head-on at gold-197 nuclei (proton number 79), and their distance of closest approach is d. Alpha particles of kinetic energy 2E_k are then fired head-on at silver-107 nuclei (proton number 47). In both cases only the electric repulsion acts and nuclear recoil is negligible. What is the new distance of closest approach?
items.why:
The two expressions look alike and are met close together, and students do not check that force (N) and energy (J) have different units. Check units: kqQ/r² gives N; kqQ/r gives N m = J. At the closest approach, E_k = kqQ/d, so d ∝ 1/E_k (not 1/√E_k).

Working: At closest approach E_k = kqQ/d, so d = k(2e)(Ze)/E_k ∝ Z/E_k. d_new/d = (47/79) × (E_k/2E_k) = 0.595 × 0.5 = 0.297, so d_new = 0.30d.
items.specStatementText: the distance of closest approach in head-on scattering experiments
items.working: At closest approach E_k = kqQ/d, so d = k(2e)(Ze)/E_k ∝ Z/E_k. d_new/d = (47/79) × (E_k/2E_k) = 0.595 × 0.5 = 0.297, so d_new = 0.30d.

items.q: In the Bohr model, the energy levels of hydrogen are E = −13.6/n² eV. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron makes a transition from n = 4 to n = 3? Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
items.why:
Forgetting to square is a common slip when substituting, especially for small n where the difference seems minor. Substitute n² explicitly: n = 2 gives 4, n = 3 gives 9. The levels are −13.6, −3.40, −1.51, −0.85 eV, crowding together towards zero.

Working: E₄ = −13.6/4² = −0.850 eV; E₃ = −13.6/3² = −1.511 eV. ΔE = 0.661 eV × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 1.058 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. λ = hc/ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(1.058 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 1.88 × 10⁻⁶ m (infrared).
items.specStatementText: the discrete energy levels in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by E = −13.6/n² eV

items.q: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, what is the angular momentum of the electron in the n = 3 orbit? Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
items.why:
n² appears in the energy formula E = −13.6/n² eV, and students carry it over into the angular momentum condition. Keep the quantities separate: L ∝ n, r ∝ n², E ∝ −1/n². Only the angular momentum condition is the postulate; the other two follow from it.

Working: Bohr condition: L = mvr = nh/2π. For n = 3: L = 3 × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s/2π = 1.989 × 10⁻³³ J s/6.283 = 3.17 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
items.specStatementText: that the existence of quantized energy and orbits arise from the quantization of angular momentum in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by mvr = nh/2π.
items.working: Bohr condition: L = mvr = nh/2π. For n = 3: L = 3 × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s/2π = 1.989 × 10⁻³³ J s/6.283 = 3.17 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

items.q: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, why can the electron occupy only certain orbits, each with its own energy?
items.correct: Its angular momentum mvr must be a whole number n times h/2π, which allows only certain radii.
items.misconception: Each orbit can hold only a fixed number of electrons, so the electron must go where there is room.
items.why:
In chemistry students learn that shells hold 2, 8, 8, … electrons, and link the existence of shells to their capacity. Shell capacity is about how many electrons can share a level; it cannot explain why a lone electron in hydrogen has discrete energies. Bohr's postulate mvr = nh/2π does.

Working: Bohr condition: L = mvr = n(h/2π), n = 1, 2, 3, … Only radii for which this holds are allowed, and each allowed orbit has its own energy, E = −13.6/n² eV.
items.specStatementText: that the existence of quantized energy and orbits arise from the quantization of angular momentum in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by mvr = nh/2π.
items.random_wrong: Its angular momentum mvr must be n² times h/2π, to match the n² in the energy formula.
items.working: Bohr condition: L = mvr = n(h/2π), n = 1, 2, 3, … Only radii for which this holds are allowed, and each allowed orbit has its own energy, E = −13.6/n² eV.

items.q: Two discharge tubes, P and Q, each contain a single gas. The emission spectrum of each gas shows exactly four bright lines in the visible region, but none of the wavelengths of the lines from P matches any of the wavelengths of the lines from Q. A student claims that P and Q contain the same element. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The claim is wrong, because an element is identified by the wavelengths of its lines, and none match.
items.misconception: The claim is correct, because the number of lines is set by the number of electrons in an atom of the element.
items.why: Bohr-style diagrams draw each electron on its own orbit and describe each line as 'an electron jumping', so lines are counted as electrons; the hydrogen spectrum, with one electron and many lines, is rarely used to test the idea. Count transitions, not electrons. An element is identified by the WAVELENGTHS of its lines, which are fixed by the differences between its energy levels; two elements can have the same number of visible lines and still be different.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide information on the chemical composition.
items.random_wrong: P and Q may contain the same element, because a gas at a higher temperature emits its lines at shorter wavelengths.

items.q: Alpha particles scattered by a thin gold foil are counted at large angles. Up to an alpha-particle kinetic energy E₀ of a few tens of MeV, the counts agree with Rutherford's prediction, which assumes that only the electric repulsion acts. Above E₀ the counts fall below the prediction. Which statement about this result is correct?
items.correct: The distance of closest approach of an alpha particle of energy E₀ gives an estimate of the radius of the gold nucleus.
items.misconception: Below E₀ the alpha particles rebound from the nuclear surface like balls from a wall; above E₀ they break through it, so fewer return.
items.why: Everyday deflections (balls, snooker, billiards) involve contact, and many diagrams draw the nucleus as a hard sphere with alpha paths that seem to touch it; 'collision' is also used loosely for scattering. Scattering is caused by electric repulsion between the positive alpha particle and the positive nucleus, which acts at a distance and grows stronger as they get closer. Every alpha particle passing near a nucleus is deflected a little; the few that head almost straight at a nucleus are slowed to rest and pushed back before they reach it.
items.specStatementText: deviations from Rutherford scattering at high energies
items.random_wrong: Above E₀ the electric repulsion no longer acts, and the strong nuclear force alone decides how the alpha particles scatter.

items.q: In the Bohr model, the energy levels of hydrogen are given by E = −13.6/n² eV. Which statement about these energy levels is correct?
items.correct: The levels become more closely spaced as n increases, converging on E = 0, at which the electron is free.
items.misconception: The levels are equally spaced in energy, because each increase of n by one adds the same energy to the atom.
items.why:
Energy-level diagrams are often drawn schematically with evenly spaced lines, and the 'ladder' analogy used to introduce them suggests equal rungs. Read the level values, not the drawing. The measured wavelengths of an element's lines are not evenly spaced in frequency, which shows that the levels themselves are unevenly spaced.

Working: E_n = −13.6/n² eV: E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV, E₄ = −13.6/16 = −0.850 eV. Gaps: 10.2 eV, 1.89 eV, 0.66 eV, … shrinking towards zero; as n → ∞, E → 0, the energy of a free electron at rest. The ground state (n = 1) is the lowest, most negative, level.
items.specStatementText: the discrete energy levels in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by E = −13.6/n² eV
items.random_wrong: The electron needs 13.6 eV to be removed from the atom whichever level it occupies at the start.
items.working: E_n = −13.6/n² eV: E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV, E₄ = −13.6/16 = −0.850 eV. Gaps: 10.2 eV, 1.89 eV, 0.66 eV, … shrinking towards zero; as n → ∞, E → 0, the energy of a free electron at rest. The ground state (n = 1) is the lowest, most negative, level.

items.q: Could the electrons in the gold atoms have turned alpha particles back?
items.correct: No. An alpha particle has about 7300 times the mass of an electron, so an electron can deflect it only very slightly, just as a table-tennis ball cannot turn back a bowling ball.
items.misconception: The large deflections were caused by alpha particles colliding with the electrons in the gold atoms.
items.why: Electrons are the atomic particles students meet first and picture most readily as small hard objects inside the atom, and in the plum-pudding model they are the only separate particles, so a 'collision with an electron' seems the obvious cause of a deflection. The electrons are far too light. Only something much more massive than the alpha particle, carrying a large concentrated positive charge, can repel it strongly enough to reverse its direction: the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment and the discovery of the nucleus
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why did most alpha particles pass through the gold foil?
items.correct: Because almost all of each atom's volume contains no concentrated charge or mass: the foil is many atoms thick, so the alpha particles passed through the atoms themselves, not between them.
items.misconception: The alpha particles passed through the gaps between the gold atoms without going through any atom.
items.why: Students picture atoms as solid balls, as in particle diagrams of solids, so passing through a solid seems possible only via the spaces between the balls. Atoms in a solid are packed together, and the foil was many atoms thick, so every alpha particle had to cross many atoms. They passed through because each atom is mostly empty of anything massive: the nucleus fills only a tiny fraction of the atom's volume.
items.specStatementText: the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment and the discovery of the nucleus
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every nucleus contain equal numbers of protons and neutrons?
items.correct: No. Only some light nuclei (such as helium-4, carbon-12 and oxygen-16) have N = Z. Heavier nuclei have more neutrons than protons; for potassium-40, N = 21 and Z = 19.
items.misconception: The number of neutrons in a nucleus is always equal to the number of protons.
items.why: The first nuclei students draw are helium-4, carbon-12 and oxygen-16, which all have N = Z, so the pattern is over-generalized. Always work out the neutron number as N = A − Z from the notation; do not assume it equals Z.
items.specStatementText: nuclear notation ᴬ_Z X where A is the nucleon number Z is the proton number and X is the chemical symbol
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the notation ᴬ_Z X, which number is the nucleon number?
items.correct: The upper number, A. The lower number is the proton number Z, which is always the smaller of the two (except for hydrogen-1, where they are equal).
items.misconception: The lower number in the notation is the nucleon number and the upper number is the proton number.
items.why: Many periodic tables print the atomic (proton) number above the symbol and the relative atomic mass below it, the reverse of nuclear notation, so students who learned one layout swap the numbers in the other. In nuclear notation the nucleon number is the superscript and the proton number is the subscript. A check: A can never be smaller than Z.
items.specStatementText: nuclear notation ᴬ_Z X where A is the nucleon number Z is the proton number and X is the chemical symbol

items.q: Are isotopes atoms with different numbers of electrons?
items.correct: No. Atoms (or ions) that differ in their number of electrons have different charges; isotopes differ in their nuclei, in the number of neutrons.
items.misconception: Isotopes are forms of an element whose atoms have gained or lost electrons.
items.why: Isotopes and ions are both introduced as 'different forms of the same element' in chemistry, and both are described by changing a number of particles, so the two ideas are confused. An ion is an atom with extra or missing electrons; its nucleus is unchanged. An isotope is defined by its nucleus: same number of protons, different number of neutrons.
items.specStatementText: nuclear notation ᴬ_Z X where A is the nucleon number Z is the proton number and X is the chemical symbol

items.q: If gas atoms re-emit the photons they absorb, why is the absorption spectrum dark at those wavelengths?
items.correct: The absorbed energy is re-emitted in all directions (and sometimes as several lower-energy photons), so very little of it continues in the original direction towards the observer.
items.misconception: Atoms re-emit all the light they absorb in its original direction, so a gas cannot produce dark lines in the light that passes through it.
items.why: Students are taught that excited atoms return to the ground state by emitting photons, and reason that the same photons must carry on along the beam, so nothing is lost. Re-emission is random in direction, so the beam loses energy at the absorbed wavelengths; seen along the beam, those wavelengths are dark.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide evidence for discrete atomic energy levels

items.q: Can an atom absorb a photon whose energy is greater than the gap to the next level, keeping the excess?
items.correct: No (for transitions between bound levels). A photon is absorbed whole or not at all, and only if its energy exactly equals the difference between the electron's level and a higher level.
items.misconception: An atom absorbs any photon whose energy is at least as large as the gap to a higher level, and the electron keeps the extra energy.
items.why: In mechanics any energy input can be taken up, and in the photoelectric effect any photon above the threshold is absorbed, so students do not expect a photon with 'more than enough' energy to be refused. An electron in an atom can exist only at the allowed levels, so it cannot keep an arbitrary extra amount. Absorption requires hf = E_upper − E_lower exactly; only a photon energetic enough to free the electron (ionization) can be absorbed with the excess becoming kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: that photons are emitted and absorbed during atomic transitions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an electron in an atom end up with an energy between two allowed levels?
items.correct: No. In an atom the electron's energy can take only the allowed level values; there are no in-between energies.
items.misconception: An electron can absorb any amount of energy and move to a position between two allowed levels.
items.why: Classical everyday experience is continuous: a ball can be lifted to any height, so an electron seems able to rise to any energy. The line spectra show that only certain energies are possible. An electron that is given an energy which would leave it between levels cannot take that energy.
items.specStatementText: that photons are emitted and absorbed during atomic transitions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When an atom emits light, does the electron leave the atom as the photon?
items.correct: No. The electron stays in the atom, in a lower level; the photon is a separate quantum of electromagnetic energy created in the transition.
items.misconception: When an atom emits light, the electron itself leaves the atom and travels away as the photon.
items.why: Both electrons and photons are described as 'particles' emitted from atoms, and the words 'emit' and 'jump' suggest something leaving; students often confuse the two particles. An electron has mass and charge; a photon has neither. In emission the electron drops to a lower level and stays bound, and the energy it loses is carried away by a newly created photon.

items.q: Does an excited atom give out light continuously while it stays excited?
items.correct: No. A single transition emits a single photon. An electron in an excited level emits nothing until it makes a transition down to a lower level.
items.misconception: An electron in a higher energy level radiates light steadily for as long as it stays there.
items.why: Hot objects glow continuously, and in classical physics an orbiting charge radiates continuously, so students picture an excited atom as glowing steadily. Emission happens in single events: each downward transition produces one photon of energy ΔE. A lamp glows steadily only because enormous numbers of atoms are being excited and de-excited all the time.

items.q: Do strong absorption lines of an element show that it is the main constituent of a star?
items.correct: No. The strength of a line depends on the temperature and on how many atoms are in the right energy level, as well as on how much of the element there is. The presence of the lines shows only that the element is there.
items.misconception: An element whose lines are strong must be the most abundant element in the star.
items.why: It seems natural that more of a substance gives a stronger signal, and in the Sun's spectrum the lines of metals such as sodium and calcium are prominent, although the Sun is mostly hydrogen and helium. Line positions identify which elements are present. Deducing how much of each is present needs further physics (such as the temperature of the gas), not simply the darkness of the line.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide information on the chemical composition.

items.q: Which number goes into R = R₀A^(1/3)?
items.correct: The nucleon number A, because the volume depends on the number of protons AND neutrons.
items.misconception: The proton number Z is used in R = R₀A^(1/3), because Z is the number that identifies the nucleus.
items.why: Z is the number used most often (it identifies the element and gives the charge), and the symbols A and Z are easily confused. Every nucleon, proton or neutron, takes up about the same volume, so the size depends on A, the total number of nucleons.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the radius and the nucleon number for a nucleus as given by R = R₀A^(1/3) and implications for nuclear densities

items.q: What does A^(1/3) mean?
items.correct: The cube root of A: the number that, multiplied by itself three times, gives A. For A = 208, A^(1/3) = 5.92.
items.misconception: A^(1/3) means A divided by 3.
items.why: A power of one-third is read as 'a third of', a common error when fractional indices are unfamiliar. A^(1/3) = ∛A. Check with a cube: 8^(1/3) = 2 (not 2.67), because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

items.q: Is the volume of a nucleus proportional to its radius?
items.correct: No. The volume of a sphere is ⁴⁄₃πR³, so it is proportional to R³.
items.misconception: The volume of a sphere is proportional to its radius, so the cube is left out when calculating nuclear volume or density.
items.why: Forgetting to cube (or to square) is a common procedural slip when a formula is used from memory, and the radius is the quantity students have just calculated. Write V = ⁴⁄₃πR³ in full, then substitute. With R = R₀A^(1/3), R³ = R₀³A.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the radius and the nucleon number for a nucleus as given by R = R₀A^(1/3) and implications for nuclear densities

items.q: Does the strong nuclear force act over the whole atom?
items.correct: No. It is a short-range force, negligible beyond a few times 10⁻¹⁵ m, so it acts only when particles are practically touching the nucleus.
items.misconception: The strong nuclear force is long-range, reaching well beyond the nucleus, because it is the strongest force.
items.why: 'Strong' is taken to mean 'far-reaching' as well as 'large', and students do not meet a force whose range is limited before the nuclear forces. The strong force is very large at nuclear distances but falls to nothing within a few femtometres. That is why low-energy alpha particles, which stop far from the nucleus, obey Rutherford's electric-force prediction exactly.
items.specStatementText: deviations from Rutherford scattering at high energies

items.q: Are alpha particles of a few tens of MeV moving close to the speed of light?
items.correct: No. An alpha particle's rest energy is about 3700 MeV, so at 30 MeV its speed is only about 0.13c and relativistic corrections are below 1%.
items.misconception: High-energy alpha particles travel close to the speed of light, so the ordinary physics used to predict their scattering breaks down.
items.why: 'High energy' is associated in popular accounts with particle accelerators and relativity, so any high-energy particle is assumed to be relativistic. Compare the kinetic energy with the rest energy. For alpha particles, tens of MeV is small compared with about 3700 MeV, so they are far from light speed; the deviations have a different cause, the strong nuclear force.
items.specStatementText: deviations from Rutherford scattering at high energies

items.q: Which numbers give the charges in a scattering calculation?
items.correct: The proton numbers: the charge of a nucleus is Ze, because neutrons are uncharged. For an alpha particle Q = 2e, for gold Q = 79e.
items.misconception: The charge of a nucleus is found from its nucleon number, Ae.
items.why: A is usually the larger and more prominent number in the notation, and students who do not separate 'number of particles' from 'number of charged particles' use it for the charge. Only protons are charged. Use Z for charge (Coulomb's law, closest approach) and A for mass and size (R = R₀A^(1/3)).

items.q: Is the Bohr condition mvr = nh?
items.correct: No. It is mvr = nh/2π: the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2π, not of h.
items.misconception: In the Bohr model the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h, so the 2π can be dropped.
items.why: h appears on its own in E = hf and in many other formulas, so the 2π is lost when the Bohr condition is recalled. Write the condition in full: L = mvr = n(h/2π). Dropping the 2π makes every speed or radius wrong by a factor of 2π.
items.specStatementText: that the existence of quantized energy and orbits arise from the quantization of angular momentum in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by mvr = nh/2π.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every Bohr orbit have the same angular momentum?
items.correct: No. The angular momentum in orbit n is nh/2π: h/2π in the first orbit, 2h/2π in the second, and so on.
items.misconception: Every allowed orbit has the same angular momentum, h/2π; only the radius changes.
items.why: Students remember that angular momentum is 'quantized in units of h/2π' and take that single unit as the value for every orbit. Quantized means restricted to whole-number multiples of h/2π. Substitute the orbit's n: mvr = nh/2π.
items.specStatementText: that the existence of quantized energy and orbits arise from the quantization of angular momentum in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by mvr = nh/2π.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are atomic energy levels discrete because light comes in photons?
items.correct: No. The causation runs the other way: the energy levels are discrete (in Bohr's model, because angular momentum is quantized), so the photons emitted in transitions have only certain energies.
items.misconception: Energy levels are discrete because light can only be emitted in photons of certain fixed sizes.
items.why: Photons and energy levels are taught together as 'quantum' ideas, and the order of explanation is easily reversed. A photon's energy can take any value, depending on its frequency. What restricts the photons from an atom is that the levels are discrete, so only certain differences are available.
items.specStatementText: that the existence of quantized energy and orbits arise from the quantization of angular momentum in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by mvr = nh/2π.

items.q: Do the wavelengths of an element's spectral lines change when the gas is hotter?
items.correct: No. The wavelengths are fixed by the differences between the atom's energy levels, which do not depend on temperature. A hotter gas may show more lines, or brighter lines, but the existing lines stay at the same wavelengths.
items.misconception: A gas at a higher temperature emits its lines at shorter wavelengths, so the same element can give different line wavelengths at different temperatures.
items.why: A heated filament changes colour from red to white as it gets hotter, and the rule 'hotter means shorter wavelength' is learned for the continuous spectrum of a hot solid, then carried over to the line spectrum of a gas. Separate the two kinds of spectrum. A hot solid emits a continuous spectrum whose peak moves with temperature; a low-pressure gas emits lines whose wavelengths are set by the atom's energy levels and are the same at any temperature.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide information on the chemical composition.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an element be identified from the overall colour of its glowing gas?
items.correct: Not reliably. The eye blends all the lines into one colour, and different elements can look similar. Identification uses a spectrometer to record the wavelengths of the individual lines and compares them with laboratory spectra.
items.misconception: Each element glows with its own characteristic colour, so the colour of the glowing gas identifies the element.
items.why: GCSE flame tests (sodium yellow, copper green) and the colours of gas-discharge signs teach that a colour goes with an element, so the blended colour is taken to be the identifying feature. The identifying feature is the pattern of line wavelengths, not the blended colour. Two gases that glow the same colour to the eye can show completely different lines in a spectrometer.
items.specStatementText: that emission and absorption spectra provide information on the chemical composition.

items.q: When an alpha particle reaches the range of the strong nuclear force, does the electric force stop acting?
items.correct: No. The electric repulsion between the alpha particle and the nucleus acts at every separation. Within a few femtometres the short-range strong nuclear force acts as well, so the net force is the sum of the two.
items.misconception: Once an alpha particle is close enough for the strong nuclear force to act, the electric force stops acting and the strong force alone determines what happens.
items.why: The two forces are taught in separate chapters, and phrases such as 'the strong force takes over' suggest a hand-over from one force to the other rather than two forces acting together. Forces add. The electric repulsion never switches off; at small separations the strong force is added to it, and it is this extra, short-range force that makes the electric-only Rutherford prediction fail.

items.q: Is the energy needed to ionize a hydrogen atom always 13.6 eV?
items.correct: No. 13.6 eV is the energy needed from the ground state, n = 1. From a higher level the electron is already nearer to E = 0, so less is needed: 3.40 eV from n = 2, 1.51 eV from n = 3.
items.misconception: An electron in any level of a hydrogen atom needs 13.6 eV to be removed from the atom.
items.why: 'The ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV' is memorized as a single fact about the element, without attaching it to the ground state in particular. The energy needed to free the electron is 0 − E_n = 13.6/n² eV, which depends on the level it starts from. Only for n = 1 is it 13.6 eV.
items.specStatementText: the discrete energy levels in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by E = −13.6/n² eV
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the Bohr model, is the n = 1 level of hydrogen the highest energy level, because 13.6 eV is the largest value?
items.correct: No. The energies are negative: E₁ = −13.6 eV is the LOWEST (most negative) energy, the ground state. Higher levels are less negative, closer to zero.
items.misconception: The n = 1 level is the highest energy level of hydrogen, because 13.6 eV is the biggest of the level values.
items.why: The minus sign is treated as a label rather than as part of the value, so the size of the number is compared instead of the number itself; ground-state values are also often quoted without the sign ('the ionization energy is 13.6 eV'). Place the levels on a number line: −13.6 eV lies below −3.40 eV, which lies below 0. A bound electron has negative energy, and the most tightly bound state has the most negative energy.
items.specStatementText: the discrete energy levels in the Bohr model for hydrogen as given by E = −13.6/n² eV
